strengths: The benchmark resource itself is substantial and carefully constructed: 403 problems from 72 contests across 14 Informatics Olympiads (2023-2025), with expert-designed private test cases, subtask rubrics, and an offline, self-contained evaluation judge validated by executing official solutions as ground truth (Appendix A.2).

Direct human comparison is a genuine differentiator: contestant rankings, medal cutoffs, and Codeforces ELO ratings enable fine-grained model-vs-human assessment (percentile, medals, Elo), which is more informative than pass rate alone, and the paper argues this well with the GPT-OSS-120B vs. Gemini-2.5-Pro example (Table 2 vs. pass rate).

Broad evaluation of 32 models across proprietary, open-weight thinking, and non-thinking categories, with useful secondary analyses: algorithm-tag breakdown (Table 3), subtask-position analysis (Fig. A2), quarterly pass-rate analysis arguing no contamination near knowledge cutoffs (Fig. A3), parallel/sequential scaling (Figs. 2, A4), submission-status error analysis (Fig. 4), and LLM-annotated reasoning-trace behavior analysis (Fig. 3).

Contamination mitigation is taken seriously: restriction to post-2022 contests, empirical check of quarterly performance trends around model cutoffs, and a concrete plan for continuous updates from 14 actively maintained competition websites.

Reproducibility efforts are real: offline judge, public data/code commitments, documented construction pipeline (crawlers, markdown conversion, quality checks of 40 sampled tasks), and detailed model/prompt information in Appendices B and E.
weaknesses: The 'private test cases' claim is weakened by the construction pipeline: test cases are scraped from official websites and supplemented from public platforms (CSES, LibreOJ, GitHub). These artifacts are publicly accessible, so a determined contamination strategy (crawling the same sources) is possible; the paper does not quantify how many problems rely on secondary-platform tests versus official releases.

The headline result (GPT-5 at 81.76th percentile) is computed from best-of-8 sampled solutions (pick the highest score), not single submissions. This conflates model capability with sampling budget and likely inflates percentiles; the paper does not report the single-sample (Pass@1) human percentile alongside, making the headline claim hard to interpret and somewhat misleading.

The reasoning-trace analysis relies on GPT-OSS-120B as the annotator for behavior categories (Sec. 5.2), which is itself one of the evaluated models. There is no human validation of the LLM annotations (e.g., agreement statistics on a sample), so conclusions such as 'stronger models allocate reasoning more strategically' rest on unverified machine labels.

Novelty is bounded by concurrent work the paper itself acknowledges (OI-Bench, LiveCodeBench Pro, HLCE, AetherCode): the core idea of Olympiad-sourced problems with human comparisons already exists; the incremental contributions (offline judge, subtask rubrics, multi-Olympiad coverage) are useful but modest. This makes ICML main track a questionable fit relative to a datasets/benchmarks venue.

Several evaluation details are underspecified or questionable: which language models are prompted to output (apparently C++), temperature/decoding settings, how problems with multiple valid outputs and interactive graders handle model solutions, and the robustness of the Gemini-based markdown conversion (only 40 tasks manually inspected) to subtle statement corruption that could shift scores.

The Elo methodology involves nontrivial filtering (rating >= 500, polynomial outlier removal, minimum 15 rated contestants) whose sensitivity is not analyzed; some matched contestant counts are very small (e.g., 5-10 per Croatian contest in Table A6), and the percentile/Elo results for such contests are noisy, with no confidence intervals reported.

The 'continuous, contamination-free updates' and leaderboard are promises rather than demonstrated artifacts at review time (the website URL is blank on the title page), so the community benefit of the live component cannot be verified.

Some analyses are descriptive rather than rigorous: the reasoning-behavior differences (Figures 3a-d) are correlational share-of-token observations without statistical testing, and causal language ('correct solutions depend heavily on initial structured planning') overreaches what the data support.

strengths: The dataset itself is a genuine asset: 403 problems drawn from 72 contests across 14 official Informatics Olympiads (2023–2025), with expert-designed private test cases (~60 per problem) and subtask rubrics, which addresses the well-documented false-positive problem in Codeforces-sourced benchmarks.

Direct integration of human contestant results (percentile, medals, Codeforces Elo via the CodeElo formula) enables meaningful model-vs-human calibration, an evaluation dimension most prior benchmarks lack.
A self-contained offline evaluation judge removes dependence on online platforms, improving accessibility and reproducibility relative to LiveCodeBench Pro and CodeElo.

The evaluation effort is substantial: 32 models spanning proprietary, open-weight thinking, and non-thinking categories, with per-algorithm-tag breakdowns (Table A9/A10), inference-time scaling analyses, and a temporal pass-rate check for contamination signals.

The construction pipeline is described in reasonable procedural detail (crawling, markdown conversion, solution verification against official solutions, Elo filtering), and problem statements like the Nile example show the tasks are authentic and well-specified.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to concurrent work. The paper itself acknowledges OI-Bench (Zhu et al., 2025), LiveCodeBench Pro, HLCE, and AetherCode. The claimed 'first' framing is contestable, and the differentiators (subtask rubrics, human percentiles, offline judge) are incremental over USACO-style prior work; Table 1's feature checklist does not establish that these differences matter empirically.

The central resource is not verifiably available. The 'Website:' field on page 1 is empty, and all data/code/leaderboard releases are stated as promises ('will be made publicly available'). For a benchmark paper, the artifact is the contribution; without a link, reproducibility and the 'Live Updates' claim rest entirely on trust.

Data quality relies heavily on LLMs with thin human validation. Gemini-2.0-Flash performs markdown conversion verification, semantic tag matching, and difficulty/label inference; contestant result CSVs are generated by pasting raw pages into Gemini-2.5-Pro. The only reported manual inspection is a 40-task sample. Error rates for these LLM-mediated steps are never quantified, yet the benchmark's claims of evaluation rigor depend on them.

The contamination argument is weaker than claimed. The cut-off is by contest year label, but Table A5 shows e.g. 'USA Computing Olympiad 2023 December_Contest' dated 2022-12-15 and several 2023-labeled contests held in late 2024/2025; conversely, problems from 2023 fall within the training windows of frontier models (GPT-5's late-2024 cutoff per Figure A3). The 'no contamination' conclusion from quarterly pass rates of only four models is an absence-of-evidence argument.

The reasoning-trace analysis (Section 5.2, Figure 3) is built on GPT-OSS-120B annotating reasoning traces, including its own. There is no human validation of the eight behavior categories or the segmentation scheme, and the reported token-share percentages are purely correlational; causal language ('stronger models strategically allocate...', 'correct solutions depend heavily on initial structured planning') is not supported by any intervention or controlled comparison, and shares are not normalized for trace length or task type.

The Elo and percentile methodology introduces unquantified noise: contestants are matched to Codeforces profiles via Google search on names/countries with 'skipped' unmatched cases, outliers removed by a fitted polynomial, and contests with <15 rated participants dropped, but no accuracy estimate for the matching step is reported. Since human percentile is the headline metric, this matters.

Some headline claims are asserted rather than demonstrated: 'eliminates high false-positive rates' is never tested against a baseline test suite; 'OpenAI models lie on the token-efficiency frontier' is a qualitative reading of Figure 1 without statistical treatment across heterogeneous model configurations.

The paper is a benchmark/evaluation study with limited methodological content beyond curation; its natural home is a datasets-and-benchmarks venue, and for an ICML main-track paper the analytical contributions (scaling, trace shares, error taxonomies) largely reconfirm known findings (reasoning helps, DP is hard).

strengths: The benchmark is genuinely well-motivated and addresses real gaps in competitive-programming evaluation: expert-designed test suites (vs. LLM/rule-generated tests), subtask-level partial scoring, direct human-contestant comparisons, and an offline judge that avoids dependence on online platforms.

The dataset construction is documented in detail (72 contests across 14 Olympiads, 403 problems, ~60 test cases/problem), with sensible quality-assurance steps: executing official solutions as ground truth to validate the judge, discarding problems with invalid solutions, and handling batch/interactive/output-only problem types separately.

Benchmarking is extensive: 32 models with multiple complementary metrics (pass rate, relative score, human percentile, medals, Elo), and the finding that GPT-OSS-120B achieves a higher pass rate than Gemini-2.5-Pro but lower percentile/Elo nicely illustrates why pass rate alone is insufficient.

The analyses go beyond a leaderboard: per-algorithm-tag breakdowns, subtask-position effects, temporal analysis against knowledge cutoffs (no evidence of contamination), parallel vs. sequential inference scaling, error-type distributions, and a reasoning-behavior taxonomy applied to traces.
The 'no temporal degradation around knowledge cutoffs' analysis (Fig. A3) is a useful contamination check that many benchmark papers omit.
weaknesses: The availability artifacts are not verifiable at review time: the 'Website:' field on the title page is literally blank, and all data, code, and leaderboard results are only promised for the future. Several headline claims (official/public test cases, reproducible offline evaluation) therefore cannot be checked by reviewers or readers yet.

The claim of 'expert-designed private tests sourced directly from official competition organizers' is overstated: Section 3 and Appendix A.1 admit substantial supplementation from CSES, LibreOJ, GitHub, and LLM-inferred metadata (Gemini-2.0-Flash fills missing tags/difficulty). Table 1's checkmarks ('official and public', 'Expert Test Cases') gloss over these caveats, and the Easy/Medium/Hard difficulty buckets inherit the noise of LLM-inferred difficulty scores.

The central human-comparison protocol favors models: models generate 8 candidates and submit the solution with the highest judged score, i.e., they receive per-problem oracle test feedback that human contestants never had within a contest. This asymmetry weakens the headline conclusion that GPT-5 (81.76th percentile) 'falls short of top human contestants'; a single-shot comparison should also be reported, and no variance/significance analysis over contests is provided.

Elo and contestant matching rely on name/country matching via Google Search to Codeforces profiles, with no reported accuracy of the matching; several contests in Table A6 have only 5-7 matched contestants, and USACO (132 tasks, the largest single source) has no human results at all, so percentile claims rest on a partially matched, contest-biased subset (46 of 72 contests).

The reasoning-trace analysis (Section 5.2) uses GPT-OSS-120B as the annotator of behavior segments, with no human validation of annotation precision reported; conclusions like 'stronger models allocate tokens more strategically' are correlational, and the suggested causal takeaways are speculative.

Ethical treatment is not addressed: automatically linking named (mostly minor) Olympiad contestants to Codeforces profiles and publishing ratings/percentiles raises privacy concerns that the paper does not discuss, nor is there a limitations section.

Novelty is incremental given concurrent work (OI-Bench, AetherCode, HLCE, LiveCodeBench-Pro, CodeELO); the comparative Table 1 is self-graded and a few entries (e.g., USACO marked non-'Updates' despite monthly releases) invite scrutiny.
